neighbours.label: the closing slot of a stock phrase or cliché ('you have to start somewhere', 'what are you waiting for', 'the chicken or the egg'), as against literal sentences using the same words
fire: Nobody is perfect on day one, but everyone has to start somewhere.
The sale ends tonight, so what are you waiting for?
Did the crime cause the poverty, or was it the chicken and the egg?
I know the first draft is rough, but you have to start somewhere.
Doctors still argue which came first - the stress or the illness.
When the tyre burst on the motorway, all he could say was 'Why me?'
The doors are open and the coffee is hot, so what are you waiting for?
Better late than never, she said, and handed in the essay.
quiet: Nobody was in the office on day one, so we sat in the hall.
The sale ends tonight at nine in the main hall.
The farmer fed the chickens and collected the eggs.
I printed the first draft and left it on your desk.
Doctors measured the stress hormones in each patient.
When the tyre burst on the motorway, he pulled over and called a garage.
The doors are open and the coffee is hot in the kitchen.
She handed in the essay late on Friday afternoon.

predictions: fire 0.3-0.6 at the hinge or end of a cliché; literal uses of the same words below 0.25, though the pole is broad
notes: Card: broad (4.0%); 'what are you waiting on?', 'start somewhere', 'First In, First Out', 'which came first - the chicken or the egg', 'Why me?'. Probe: 'Which came first - the chicken' 0.627, 'start somewhere' 0.566, 'waiting on?' 0.501, 'same reaction' 0.213; 'the student who failed' 0.110 but 'cat slept on the mat' 0.318 and milk floor 0.209, so near misses may leak.
